extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys, and applicants dealing with Korean patentability requirements
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining and determining patentability under the Korean Patent Act, covering industrial applicability, novelty, inventive step, enlarged novelty concepts, and unpatentable subject matter. Includes definitions, examples, examination procedures, and refusal-notification guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial applicability (Patent Act Article 29(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions that have industrial applicability are patentable unless they fall under prior-publication/work or publication-through-telecommunication exceptions (Article 29(1) subparagraphs). 'Industry' is interpreted broadly to cover all useful activities and practical technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An invention must be both an 'invention' and industrially applicable. Examiner should indicate specific grounds when finding lack of industrial applicability. See Paris Convention reference that industrial property is broadly understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory invention (Patent Act Article 2(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'Invention' means the highly advanced creation of a technical idea using the rules of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Highly advanced creation' is a relative concept (distinguishes Patent from Utility Model) but is not considered in practice when determining whether a claimed subject matter meets the requirements of 'Invention' for patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: A law of nature as such (non-statutory invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: A law of nature (e.g., second law of thermodynamics) as such is not considered a statutory invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claimed subject matter is merely a natural law, it is non-statutory and should be refused under industrial applicability grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere discoveries and not creations (non-statutory invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere discoveries (finding laws or natural things) are not creations and thus not statutory inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolated/artificially separated natural things (chemical substances, microorganisms) and methods of isolation can be statutory. New use inventions require non-obvious inventive activity closely related to the newly found property to be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Those contrary to a law of nature (non-statutory invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that involve means contrary to a law of nature (e.g., perpetual motion) are not statutory inventions because an invention must utilize a law of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any means necessary to define the claimed invention contradict natural laws, the claimed invention is non-statutory (cite relevant court decisions where applicable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Those in which a law of nature is not utilized (non-statutory invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that use non-natural-law principles (economic rules, pure mathematical methods, logic, cartography rules, arbitrary arrangements, or mental activities such as business methods or teaching skills) are not statutory inventions unless the claim as a whole utilizes a law of nature via technical devices or methods producing useful, concrete, tangible results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the claimed invention as a whole — even if some claim parts don't utilize natural laws, the whole may be statutory if it uses technical means to produce objective, repeatable results. Examples provided (cryptograph design method, phonetic transcription method, garbage recycling management method) illustrate borderline cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill (personal skill not statutory)
rubrics_metrics.description: A personal skill acquired by practice (lacking objectivity and transferrable instruction) is not a statutory invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: methods of performing musical instruments or throwing techniques defined only by a performer's practice are non-statutory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere presentation of information (non-statutory invention)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere presentation of information where the technical feature resides solely in content and the main objective is to present information is not statutory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: audio CDs (music content), program listings, raw image data. However, presentation per se, means for presentation, or methods/means that embody technical features (e.g., a plastic card with embossed info) can be statutory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic creations (non-statutory unless technical means used)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure aesthetic creations (paintings, carvings) are not statutory inventions, but where aesthetic result is achieved by technical composition or technical means, it may be statutory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation is subjective; determine whether technical means produce the aesthetic result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer programming language or computer program (non-statutory unless tied to hardware/machine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer programs as mere lists of orders are not statutory inventions. But inventions where data processing is specifically executed using hardware (data-processing unit/machine operating with the program), the operating method, or computer-readable media carrying the program are statutory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for a concrete hardware association, operating method, or novel machine-readable medium to treat software-related claims as statutory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Those whose outcome of the claimed subject matter is not achievable (non-statutory)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention whose claimed outcome is not achievable and reproducible is not statutory even if means are described; reproducibility need not be 100% but must be reasonably certain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must assess whether it's 'certain that the outcome is achievable' given the description and state of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incomplete invention (non-statutory)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statutory invention must be complete: subject matters must be specified clearly and thoroughly so a person of ordinary skill can easily replicate to achieve the intended technical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish completeness (cannot be cured after filing) from deficiencies in description (can sometimes be amended). If unclear whether incomplete or deficient description, prefer refusal under Article 42(3). Evidence (reliable experimental data) can be used by applicant to verify the invention solves the stated problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification of reason for refusal for non-statutory inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application falls within non-statutory categories (law of nature, discovery, contrary-to-nature, not utilizing natural law, mere information, aesthetic, incomplete), the reason for refusal shall be notified citing that the invention does not involve 'inventions that have industrial applicability' (main paragraph of Article 29(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should state reasons specifically when notifying refusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between statutory invention (Patent Act) and device (Utility Model Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Act allows devices and methods; Utility Model Act grants protection only for devices that relate to shape or construction of an article or combination of articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For utility model eligibility, consider whether subject matter is an 'article' with shape and use, construction (3D spatial), or a 'combination' of articles. Processes, compositions, chemical materials, non-fixed things, and plant/animal varieties do not fall under Utility Model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrially inapplicable inventions — medical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods for treatment of the human body by surgery or therapy and diagnostic methods practiced on the human body are considered industrially inapplicable (not patentable). Methods including medical activities even as part of steps are inapplicable. Methods whose purpose mixes therapeutic and non-therapeutic effects (e.g., cosmetic) or where therapeutic vs non-therapeutic effects cannot be separated are treated as surgical/therapeutic methods and inapplicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical devices and products themselves are industrially applicable. Methods operating a medical device or measurement methods are applicable when separable from practical medical activities. Methods limited to animals (not human) may be industrially applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrially inapplicable inventions — cannot be commercialized
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions only for personal use, academic or experimental purposes are regarded as industrially inapplicable. Marketable or tradable subject matter is considered industrially applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess commercializability/marketability when deciding industrial applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrially inapplicable inventions — cannot be implemented
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention that cannot be implemented or practiced in reality is not industrially applicable even if it works in theory. However, inventions not yet used at filing may be industrially applicable if use in the industry in the future is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not deem inventions industrially applicable solely because future technology might advance; need realistic potential to be used in industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (Article 29(1)) — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention lacks novelty if it was publicly known or worked, described in a publication, or published through electric telecommunication lines before the filing date (Article 29(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time of filing is exact point (hour/minute) converted to Korean time. Prior public disclosure anywhere (domestic or foreign) may be prior art. Examiner uses categories of prior art: publicly known, publicly worked, distributed publications, electric telecommunication disclosure. See revisions expanding 'publicly known' to outside Korea for applications filed on/after 2006-10-01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicly known invention (novelty subcriterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention whose contents have been known to unspecified persons without secrecy obligation prior to filing is 'publicly known'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Unspecified persons' means general public; use exact filing time. If an application is not laid open/published, it is not prior art under Article 29(1)(2) though may be under other provisions once publicly inspectable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicly worked invention (novelty subcriterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention that has been worked under conditions in which its contents are or can potentially be publicly known is 'publicly worked'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if inner parts remain secret, if a person skilled could learn the invention by observing or being allowed to inspect/explain inner parts (and not refused), it can be publicly worked. If inner parts remain secret and not accessible, it may not be publicly worked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention described in a distributed publication (novelty subcriterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A publication (document/drawing/medium duplicated for disclosure) placed such that unspecified persons can read/see it is a distributed publication and constitutes prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribution means making available for unspecified persons; further guidance addresses distribution timing, content, and what counts as distribution (including electronic distribution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventions distributed to the public via electric telecommunication lines (novelty subcriterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information published through electric telecommunication lines may be cited as prior art if it meets requirements prescribed by Presidential Decree and guidelines (Article 29(1)(2) variant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance covers purport, requirements for information to be considered available to the public, finding time of publication and content, methods of citation, and matters needing attention when applying these guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the identity of claimed inventions (novelty assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure and principles for defining the invention in claims and finding the identity between claimed invention and cited inventions when determining novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes methods for defining inventions disclosed in claims (general principle and handling special expressions), finding cited inventions (publicly known/worked/published), determining novelty for numerical/parameter-limited inventions, and general considerations. Identity includes substantial identity; do not combine more than two cited inventions when comparing to a single claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventions not considered publicly known (Article 30) — exceptions and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Article 30, certain disclosures by persons with the right to apply (e.g., laid open by inventor before filing) may not be treated as public knowledge for novelty purposes, subject to conditions and procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance details purport, requirements, distinctions between disclosures made by the applicant intentionally or against their intention, procedural steps to take advantage of Article 30, formality and substantial examinations, and matters to attend when applying Article 30.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlarged concept of novelty (Article 29(3) & (4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisions treating inventions described in other applications (prior or subsequent) as if filed on the filing date under certain conditions; includes conditions to meet, guidelines applying proviso, and handling of international applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers conditions (another application laid open/published, identity of invention in claims vs initial specification, priority issues), procedure for determining identity, and special rules for international applications and domestic priority claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step (Article 29(2)) — general principle
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention has inventive step if it would not have been obvious to a person skilled in the art in light of prior art before filing (Article 29(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance includes defining person skilled in the art, prior to filing, inventions easily made, general principles for determination, and a detailed method of determining inventive step including selection of cited inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of determining inventive step — procedure and selection of cited invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural steps for evaluating inventive step and principles for selecting which cited inventions to use as starting points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes concrete methods and precautions when selecting cited inventions (do not improperly combine, consider what the person skilled would actually do).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable cause or motivation (inventive step factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Probable cause or motivation to combine or modify prior art (e.g., suggestions in disclosures, close similarity of problem or function, close relation of technical fields) supports obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subfactors: suggestions shown in disclosures of cited inventions; close similarity of a problem to be solved; close similarity of function/work/operation; close relation of technical fields. Use these to assess whether combination would be obvious to skilled person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere exercise of ordinary creativity (inventive step negative indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes that amount to routine work by a person skilled in the art (replacement with equivalents, workshop modifications, partial removal of technical features, simple changes/limitations, general application of known art) do not impart inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete sub-examples provided: replacement with equivalents, workshop modification of a design, partial removal of features, simple change/limit of use, general application of known art. Examiner should distinguish routine adaptation from inventive contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantageous effects to be considered (inventive step positive indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider advantageous effects produced by claimed features when assessing inventive step; beneficial technical effects can support non-obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether claimed advantages are credible, supported by description or evidence, and not merely result of routine optimization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining inventive step according to invention type
rubrics_metrics.description: Different guidance for selection inventions, inventions with numerical limitations, parameter inventions, and product inventions described by their manufacturing process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific methods for each invention type: e.g., selection inventions require assessment of whether selection is non-obvious; numerical and parameter inventions require attention to ranges, boundary values, reproducibility; products described by manufacturing processes require linking product properties to process steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of inventive step of a combination invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Special considerations when the claimed invention is a combination of known elements — whether the combination yields a new technical effect or merely aggregates known features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess synergy, whether combination yields non-obvious effects, and whether prior art provided motivation to combine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other factors to be taken into account in determining obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional considerations beyond the main factors (e.g., common general knowledge, expectations in the field, secondary indicia) when assessing inventive step/obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes notes on evidence, context, and field-specific practices; see chapter sections for examples and examiner notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpatentable invention — contravene public order or morality (Article 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding Articles 29(1)-(2), an invention likely to contravene public order or morality may not be patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public order refers to general societal interest; morality means generally accepted moral sense. Consider both the aim of the invention and its disclosure/use; improper use contrary to original purpose is not by itself sufficient. Provide concrete analysis in notification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpatentable invention — injure public health (Article 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention likely to injure public health is unpatentable under Article 32 and should be treated similarly to inventions contravening public order or morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When manufacturing-process inventions are involved, consider both the process and the product. Official regulatory approval (e.g., Ministry of Health and Welfare) may be relevant. Consider whether methods exist to eliminate harmful effects or whether advantages outweigh harms.
